title: Alain Badiou
keyWorks: Ethics: An Essay on the Understanding of Evil (1993)
summary: Alain Badiou is a French philosopher for whom the heart of life is the "event": an unexpected encounter, discovery or rupture after which the world can no longer stay the same. A person truly becomes a subject when they remain "faithful" to such an event and build their life out of it. Badiou identifies four domains in which truths are born: love, art, science and politics.
onEmotions: Badiou is not a psychologist and hardly writes about feelings as inner states. What interests him is what a person does when something happens to them that goes beyond the usual order of things. In his early Theory of the Subject, drawing on Lacan, he names four "affects" of the subject: anxiety, the superego, courage and justice. For Badiou, feelings are often signs that something new has broken into a life, or that a person is wavering between their habitual life and fidelity to this new thing. His view is supportive: even a difficult feeling can be a sign that you are living not only to survive, but for something greater.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is a heavy but understandable feeling, and you don't need to be ashamed of it. Badiou gave it a place in Theory of the Subject, where, following Lacan, he described anxiety as one of the four fundamental affects of the subject. Anxiety, for Badiou, arises when the usual order of things breaks down and something breaks into life that we don't yet have a name for. It is a sign of a collision with the new. But in the same book Badiou names another affect — courage: the ability to act without complete certainty. From this point of view, your anxiety is not a verdict but a possible threshold. It tells you that something is changing. You don't need to get rid of it at once; alongside it you can find a little courage for one small step.
anxiety.practice: Ask yourself: what new or unknown thing has broken into my life right now? And what is the smallest step I could take towards it?

fear.text: Fear is a natural reaction to the unknown, and it doesn't make you weak. Badiou did not think courage is the absence of fear. In Theory of the Subject, courage is described as the capacity to hold on to the new when your usual footing has vanished. For Badiou, most of our life takes place within the order of the "situation" — the world of the familiar, where everything is known and assigned its place. An event disrupts this order, and fear is a normal response to such a disruption. From this point of view, one could say that your fear may indicate that you are facing something truly important. Courage doesn't require you to stop being afraid. It only invites you not to let fear decide everything for you.
fear.practice: Name your fear and finish the sentence: "If fear weren't deciding for me, I would…". You don't have to do it — just notice the answer.

sadness.text: Sadness is a legitimate feeling, and there is no need to hide it. Badiou didn't write about sadness as such, but from the standpoint of his thought something important can be said. He distinguished the life of the "human animal", concerned with survival and pleasures, from the life of a subject bound to something greater — love, creative work, a shared cause, the search for truth. Sadness often appears when we feel that life has been reduced to routine and that this something greater is missing. Such sadness is not a weakness but a longing for meaning. Badiou believed that every person has the capacity to become a subject of truth. Your sadness may be a reminder of this capacity — that you need not only comfort, but something genuine.
sadness.practice: Ask yourself: what "greater" thing, beyond everyday concerns, is my sadness longing for right now?

grief.text: Grief is a deep experience of loss, and it deserves time and respect. Badiou's central concept is "fidelity to the event": the capacity to go on living out of what once changed your life, even when the event itself lies in the past. From this point of view, one could say: if you have lost a person, or something that was an event for you — a love, a friendship, a shared cause — the loss does not cancel what happened. The event took place, and it goes on acting through you: through the way you see the world, what you value, how you live. Grief is the price of that bond. Fidelity to what was lost doesn't have to mean freezing in pain; it can mean carrying forward what you were given.
grief.practice: Think about it: what did the person or experience you lost change in you forever? Write down one such change.

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts, and the fact that you feel it speaks of a living need for connection. Badiou thought a great deal about the passage from "the One" to "the Two". In In Praise of Love he describes love as a "scene of the Two": an experience in which the world begins to be seen not from one point of view but from two. But Badiou stresses something else too: the truths born in love, art, science and politics are universal — they are addressed to everyone. From this point of view, one could say that even in loneliness you are not cut off from what is shared. When you read a book, listen to music or think through a real question, you take part in something that connects people. And loneliness can become a waiting for an encounter — an openness to an event.
loneliness.practice: Recall a book, song or idea that made you feel connected to someone far away. Return to it today, even for a couple of minutes.

anger.text: Anger is a legitimate feeling: often it tells you that something just has been violated. Badiou named justice as one of the four affects of the subject. But in Ethics he also warns about forms of evil that arise when fidelity to something great turns into destruction: when, for the sake of their truth, a person is ready to destroy others. He calls this the "terror" and "disaster" of truth. From this point of view, your anger is valuable as a signal of injustice, but its force calls for clarity. Badiou would help you tell apart anger that strives for justice for everyone from anger that only wants to win or take revenge. The first can become a source of faithful action; the second tends to wear out both you and others.
anger.practice: Ask yourself: what does my anger want — justice that would be good for everyone, or only for someone to feel bad?

shame.text: Shame is an agonizing feeling, and you deserve to treat yourself gently within it. Badiou didn't write about shame specifically, but from the standpoint of his Ethics something supportive can be said. He criticized seeing a human being only as a weak creature, a victim to be protected and assessed. For Badiou, every person has a capacity for something more: to become a subject bound to a truth — in love, in creative work, in thought, in a shared cause. Shame often reduces us to one mistake or one trait, as if our whole essence lay in it. Badiou invites you to see a person differently: as someone capable of fidelity, of a new beginning. Your mistake doesn't define your whole life — you are more than what you are ashamed of.
shame.practice: Write down one thing you remain faithful to no matter what — a person, a cause, a value. That is part of you too.

guilt.text: Guilt tells you that you care, and that in itself is valuable. In Ethics, Badiou calls one form of evil "betrayal" — giving up fidelity to an event that once changed your life: a love, a cause, a discovery. But in his view fidelity is not a flawless past; it is something that can be renewed. A subject is not created once and for all, but with each new decision to keep going. From this point of view, one could say that if you feel guilty for stepping back from something important, it doesn't mean all is lost. The guilt itself shows that the bond with that important thing is still alive. You can turn it not into self-punishment but into a return — the next step of fidelity.
guilt.practice: Ask yourself: what important thing do I feel I have stepped back from? What small step would help me return to it?

envy.text: Envy is an unpleasant but very human feeling, and admitting to it is honest. Badiou, following Lacan, spoke of the "service of goods" — a life built around acquiring, owning and comparing. In that world there will always be someone who has more. But the truths Badiou writes about work differently: they belong to no one and don't diminish when they are shared. Someone else's love doesn't take away your ability to love; someone else's discovery doesn't close off yours. From this point of view, one could say that envy is tormenting as long as we live by the logic of goods. But it can point to what really matters to you — and then the question is no longer "why do they have it and I don't" but "what do I want to be faithful to?".
envy.practice: Look at what you envy and ask: is it a good that can be owned, or a cause that one can devote oneself to?

emptiness.text: A sense of emptiness is hard, and it deserves attention rather than reproach. Badiou might explain it like this: a life without an event is a life reduced to keeping oneself going — to work, rest and consumption. In Logics of Worlds he describes a widespread conviction of our time: that there are only bodies and languages, and nothing more. Badiou adds: "except that there are truths." From this point of view, one could say that your emptiness is not an emptiness of you yourself, but a sense that nothing truly new has happened in your life for a long time. Badiou doesn't suggest manufacturing events artificially — they arrive unexpectedly. But you can stay open to them: to an encounter, an idea, a cause that might suddenly take hold of you.
emptiness.practice: Recall the last time something truly took hold of you — a meeting, a book, an idea. What was different then?

confusion.text: Confusion is a natural reaction to what goes beyond the familiar, and there is nothing shameful in it. Badiou might even say that confusion often accompanies an event. An event, in his view, is "undecidable": at the moment it happens, it cannot be proven that it truly matters. A first meeting, an unexpected thought, a sharp turn — all of these at first bring disarray. There are no rules to tell you what to do. That is why, for Badiou, a subject is born out of a decision, a kind of wager — a choice made without full certainty. From this point of view, your confusion is not an absence of bearings but a sign that you are facing something new. Clarity will come not before the decision, but through it.
confusion.practice: Ask yourself: what new circumstance has thrown off my usual bearings? What do I already feel about it, even without certainty?

fatigue.text: Your tiredness is real, and it doesn't diminish what you are doing. Badiou speaks of fidelity to an event as long, everyday work — not a heroic impulse but persistence over time. Such fidelity is naturally tiring. But it is worth distinguishing two kinds of tiredness: tiredness from the "service of goods" — from the endless race for possessions and status — and tiredness from fidelity to what truly matters to you. From this point of view, one could say that the first exhausts you because it has no end, while the second, for all its heaviness, is full of meaning. Badiou doesn't demand superhuman strength from you. Fidelity includes pauses and rest too — you can only keep going by taking care of yourself.
fatigue.practice: Ask yourself: what am I more tired of — the race for external things, or a cause that is truly dear to me?

boredom.text: Boredom can be tormenting, and there is nothing shameful in it. Badiou might see it as a perfectly understandable reaction to a world he describes as a "situation" — the usual order in which everything has already been counted and assigned its place, where each day is like the one before. In such a world nothing really happens. From Badiou's point of view, one could say that boredom is the sense that life consists of repetition while you are waiting for something more. And that waiting isn't empty. Badiou believed that events arrive unexpectedly, from points the order doesn't notice. Your boredom may be a form of openness — a waiting, not in vain, for something that will one day break the monotony and call you to follow it.
boredom.practice: Notice one small thing around you that you usually pay no attention to. Could there be something unexpected in it?

joy.text: Joy is a precious feeling, and it needs no justification. In his book Metaphysics of Real Happiness, Badiou distinguishes true happiness from satisfaction. Satisfaction is when our needs and comforts are met, when everything goes as it should. Happiness, for Badiou, is tied to an event: it arises when we take part in something new — in love, a discovery, creative work, a shared cause — and find in ourselves abilities we never suspected. From this point of view, your joy may be a sign that you have touched something genuine. It is worth noticing it and asking yourself where it came from. Perhaps it is not just a pleasant moment but the beginning of something you can be faithful to.
joy.practice: Ask yourself: is my joy right now the satisfaction of comfort, or the happiness of meeting something new?

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the deepest human experiences, and Badiou devoted a whole book to them — In Praise of Love. For him, love begins with an encounter — an event that cannot be predicted and that breaks through ordinary life. But the main thing is not the encounter but what follows it: the long, shared work of building a world "from the point of view of the Two". Badiou criticizes today's attempts to make love safe — free of risk and surprises, choosing a partner like a product. Love, in his view, is an adventure that demands tenacity. From this point of view, your tenderness is not just a pleasant feeling but the beginning or continuation of a truth that is created by two people. It is worth cherishing as an event that changed how you see the world.
love.practice: Think of someone you love and ask: what in the world have I come to see anew because I look at it together with them?

quote.author: Arthur Rimbaud
quote.source: A Season in Hell (Badiou quotes these words in In Praise of Love)

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling that connects you with the world. Badiou didn't write about it specifically, but from the standpoint of his thought something deep can be said. An event, for Badiou, cannot be produced, earned or planned: it happens, it arrives on its own. In his book on the apostle Paul he even uses the word "grace", freeing it from its religious sense, to name what is given without being deserved. Meeting someone you love, an unexpected idea, a book that changed your life — all of these are gifts that might never have come. Gratitude in this sense is the recognition that the best things in our lives came not only from our own efforts. This view lightens the load: you don't have to earn everything good. You can simply accept it.
gratitude.practice: Name one encounter or one event in your life that came unexpectedly and changed you for the better.

hope.text: Hope is an important feeling, and it's good that you have it. Badiou is sceptical of passively waiting for everything to sort itself out. But his philosophy is deeply hopeful: it affirms that the new is possible, that events happen even where nobody expects them, and that every person is capable of taking part in something greater. In Ethics he formulates a simple maxim for anyone who has once touched something important: "Keep going!" This is not about straining yourself but about calm persistence. From this point of view, your hope is not a dream of a future someone else will bring, but fidelity to what has already been promised to you by an encounter, a cause, a love. To hope is to keep going, even in small steps.
hope.practice: Recall what you want to stay faithful to. What is the smallest step of "keeping going" you could take today?

quote.text: Do all that you can to persevere in that which exceeds your perseverance.
quote.author: Alain Badiou
quote.source: Ethics: An Essay on the Understanding of Evil

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a warm, aching feeling, and you don't need to give it up. Badiou might offer a distinction between nostalgia and fidelity. Nostalgia faces backwards: it longs for what was and wants to bring the past back. Fidelity to an event, for Badiou, faces forwards: it takes what once happened and keeps unfolding its consequences in the present and the future. From this point of view, one could say that your nostalgia may hold the memory of an event — a love, a friendship, a time when you felt truly alive. That is a precious memory. And you can turn it from longing into a question: how can what mattered then continue in my life now?
nostalgia.practice: Think about the time you miss and ask: what event from that time can I carry on today?

craving.text: A craving can be very strong, and the fact that it's hard for you says nothing bad about you. Badiou distinguishes the "human animal", which lives by its interests, habits and needs, from the "subject" — the same person at a moment when they hold on to something greater than the immediate. This is no reproach to the animal in us: everyone has it. In Logics of Worlds, Badiou describes a "point" — a moment when the whole world seems to shrink to a simple "yes" or "no". From this point of view, one could say that an acute craving feels exactly like that: as if everything is being decided right now. But Badiou stresses that a subject is made not of one heroic gesture but of many small decisions. One wave is not the whole world, and it passes.
craving.practice: When a craving washes over you, name it aloud or to yourself: "this is a point, not the whole world." Then do one small thing — a sip of water, a few steps — and notice how the wave changes.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure or a life sentence, but a circuit that is genuinely hard to get out of. Badiou describes a world in which life is reduced to "bodies and languages", to consumption and the satisfaction of needs; he calls this "democratic materialism" and sees in it not personal guilt but the general climate of the age. From this point of view, one could say that addiction is a world that has narrowed and arranged itself around a single centre. Badiou believes that in any situation, even the most closed, something new is possible, and that truths are not built alone: for Badiou, a subject can also be collective. The way out of the circuit is not a single burst of willpower but a slow fidelity to what makes life wider again, together with other people.
addiction.practice: Write down one thing, other than what your life is currently built around, that once truly captivated you. If you wish, you can talk to someone who understands — for example, in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: The morning after can be doubly hard: your body feels bad, and inside you feel anxious and ashamed. This is an understandable reaction, and it doesn't make you a worse person. In Ethics, Badiou says that fidelity is not flawlessness but the capacity to keep going. His ethical maxim is simple: keep going, hold on to what matters to you, even if you've lost your way. From this point of view, one could say that last night doesn't define who you are. Badiou generally refuses to see a person through their weakness or through what has happened to them — he looks at what a person is capable of next. Memory gaps and awkwardness can be frightening, but today is not a continuation of yesterday's failure; it is a new chance to choose what you stay faithful to.
hangover.practice: Drink some water and calmly write one sentence: "Today I keep holding on to …" — naming what matters to you, without reproaching yourself.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria can be wonderful: the world seems open, everything is possible. There's no need to spoil it with suspicion. Badiou values such moments — he writes a great deal about how the new breaks into life and how a whole way of seeing the world changes. But he offers one distinction: an event is recognized not by the strength of its first impression, but by what is later built from it. An intense feeling may be the sign of a genuine encounter, idea or love — or it may simply be a bright moment, and there's nothing wrong with that either. From this point of view, you can calmly enjoy the high and at the same time look with curiosity: what in it is truly yours, and what will you want to carry on once the wave settles?
euphoria.practice: While the high lasts, write down one thought or image that seems important to you right now. In a couple of days, reread it and see what you want to continue.

crash.text: A comedown after a high can be very painful: a moment ago everything was bright, and now it is grey and heavy. Many people know this, and it is not a weakness of yours. Badiou described a similar rhythm in history: after bursts of the new, such as May 1968, come periods he called "Restoration" — when the familiar order returns and it seems as if nothing ever happened. But for Badiou this does not cancel the event: it took place, and its consequences keep acting. From this point of view, one could say that the comedown is not proof that the high was a deception. It is a time when the flash has ended and the slow work has not yet begun. You can let this time be, without demanding of yourself that you bring back the earlier brightness right away.
crash.practice: Name one thing from the recent high that was real and stays with you, even if you can't feel it right now.

panic.text: Panic is very frightening: your heart pounds, your breathing falters, it feels as if something irreparable is about to happen. You are not alone with this, and a wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. In Theory of the Subject, Badiou, following Lacan, describes anxiety as an encounter with something "excessive", something that doesn't fit into the familiar order. Beside it he places courage — not the absence of fear, but the capacity to stay put while something incomprehensible is happening. From this point of view, one could say that in a moment of panic you don't need to decide or understand anything. Courage here is very simple and bodily — waiting out the wave, feeling the ground under your feet and breathing, knowing that it passes.
panic.practice: Put both feet on the floor and take a few breaths with the out-breath longer than the in-breath. Name aloud five objects you can see around you.

dread.text: Existential dread — "what is it all for, if everything ends?" — is one of the heaviest experiences, and there is a lot of honesty in it. Badiou argues with philosophies that put finitude and death at the centre. He holds that a human being is defined not by being mortal, but by being able to take part in truths — in love, creative work, knowledge, a shared cause. In Ethics he even says that a human being can be "immortal": not because they won't die, but because in moments of fidelity to a truth they partake in something that goes beyond their individual life. From this point of view, the answer to "what for?" is not a formula but what you already love, understand and do together with others.
dread.practice: Recall a moment when you were completely absorbed in something — a conversation, music, a task. Write down what it held that made asking "what for?" unnecessary.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives while you are not where you should be is very common, and it is understandable. Badiou thinks a lot about what "the true life" is. The title of his book The True Life echoes a line by Rimbaud, whom Badiou loves to quote. But for Badiou the true life is not "somewhere out there", in other people's bright events. A real event, in his view, cannot be planned, bought or caught by scrolling a feed: it happens within your own situation, often where nobody is looking. From this point of view, one could say that the fear of missing out pushes you to chase other people's lives, while an event comes to the one who is open to what is happening right beside them.
fomo.practice: Write down one thing happening in your own life right now that you may be underrating because it doesn't look like other people's bright pictures.

quote.text: True life is absent. We are not in the world.
quote.author: Arthur Rimbaud

sleepless.text: Insomnia and 3 a.m. thoughts are exhausting, and it is completely understandable that this is hard for you. At night everything seems bigger and more hopeless. Badiou didn't write about insomnia, but from the standpoint of his thought something can be said. He distinguishes the "state of the situation" — the habitual order that counts everything, sorts it into boxes and evaluates it — from what does not fit into this order. Night thoughts often resemble an endless recount: what hasn't been done, what went wrong. But this recount is not the truth about you. Badiou insists that the most important things in life can't be derived from calculations. At night you can allow yourself not to solve anything, and simply put off the counting until morning.
sleepless.practice: Write your troubling thoughts on a sheet of paper and tell yourself: "This count can wait until morning." Then put a hand on your chest and feel a few slow out-breaths.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: what collapses is not only trust in a person but also what you believed in together. This pain is legitimate. In Ethics, Badiou names betrayal as one of the forms of evil — but in a special sense: it is giving up fidelity to what once changed a life, when a person convinces themselves that "nothing really happened". From this point of view, one could say something important: if someone betrayed you, it doesn't cancel what was genuine on your side. Your fidelity, your love or friendship were real. Badiou shows that betrayal is the other's renunciation, not proof that you were naive. You don't have to renounce what you saw back then and what you invested in.
betrayal.practice: Write: "What was real on my side was …" Let it remain yours, whatever the other person did.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonizing, and there is often more fear of loss in it than anger. In In Praise of Love, Badiou describes love as a "scene of the Two": two people don't merge into one, but begin to look at the world together from the point of view of difference. From this point of view, one could say that jealousy is a moment when love pulls back towards "the One": towards the wish to possess, to control, to reduce the other to yourself. This doesn't make you a bad person; it is a very understandable fear. But for Badiou love is not possession but a shared construction that rests on trust and on risk. You can acknowledge jealousy without letting it decide for you: it speaks of fear, not necessarily of the truth.
jealousy.practice: Ask yourself and write down: "What am I really afraid of losing?" Try to name it in one or two words.

resentment.text: An old grievance is heavy: you carry it with you for years, and it is understandable — you really were hurt. Badiou doesn't write directly about grievances, but in Ethics he criticizes a view in which a person is defined first and foremost as a victim — as someone to whom something was done. He doesn't deny real harm, but he holds that a person is more than their wounds: they are capable of something new. From this point of view, one could say that a grievance keeps you tied to one old situation, as if time had stopped. Badiou doesn't demand that you forgive or forget. He only reminds you that the future can't be derived from the past, and that you have a right to a life defined not only by what was done to you.
resentment.practice: Name one thing in your life that has nothing to do with this grievance. Give it a couple of minutes of attention today.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart hurts almost physically, and it is one of the strongest human pains. Badiou takes love very seriously: for him it is one of the four domains in which truth is born. In In Praise of Love he writes that love begins with an encounter — an event — and then becomes the long construction of a world seen through the eyes of two. From this point of view, one could say that a breakup interrupts this construction but does not cancel the fact that it existed. You saw the world from the point of view of the Two, and that vision has already changed you. Badiou considers love a risk you can't insure against — and that is exactly why it is precious. Your pain is the price of having taken that risk.
heartbreak.practice: Write down one thing you began to see or value differently thanks to this relationship. It stays yours.

impostor.text: The fear that you are about to be found out is familiar to very many people — even to those you admire. Badiou can be unexpectedly supportive here. For him, a subject is not someone who possesses the right qualifications in advance, but someone who holds to fidelity to something new. Truths, for Badiou, are addressed to "anyone at all": to take part in them you need no special status. The subject itself emerges in the process; it doesn't exist before it. From this point of view, one could say that the feeling of being "not the real thing" often means you are engaged in something bigger than your former role. Nobody is ever "ready" in advance. You become who you become by doing it.
impostor.practice: Write: "I am here not because I know everything, but because …" — and finish the sentence honestly.

self_hatred.text: An inner voice that judges you mercilessly can sound very convincing, but it doesn't tell the whole truth about you. In Theory of the Subject, Badiou, drawing on Lacan, names one of the affects "the superego" — the voice of a law that demands more and more, punishes, and is never satisfied. Alongside it Badiou places courage and justice — entirely different ways of relating to yourself and the world. From this point of view, one could say that the inner critic is not your conscience but a harsh mechanism that confuses high standards with cruelty. Its verdict is not final. Justice, for Badiou, concerns everyone — including you.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence the inner critic is saying right now. Then, next to it, write what a fair and kind person who could see the whole picture would say.

helplessness.text: Being powerless to change something is hard, and it is often tied to real circumstances rather than to any weakness of yours. In Logics of Worlds, Badiou introduces the concept of "the inexistent": in every world there is something that is barely visible in it, that exists only minimally. An event, for Badiou, can raise this inexistent to full existence — he recalls the line from the "Internationale": "We have been naught, we shall be all." From this point of view, one could say that what seems impossible now is not necessarily impossible forever. Badiou says that the new is often born precisely where the order declares "that can't happen". You don't have to change everything at once; sometimes it is enough to stay open.
helplessness.practice: Choose one tiny action that is within your power today — not to change everything, but simply to feel that something is within your reach.

procrastination.text: When you can't get started, it isn't laziness or a vice — often there is fear, tiredness or a sense that the task is too big behind it. Badiou describes fidelity to an event as long, everyday work: not a heroic leap but carrying on, step by step. His maxim in Ethics sounds almost homely: keep going. From this point of view, one could say that starting doesn't mean doing everything right straight away. Badiou stresses that the subject acts without guarantees: nobody knows in advance whether something will work out. Courage, in his view, is not confidence in success but a readiness to take a step when there is no certainty. Sometimes that step is very small.
procrastination.practice: Choose the smallest part of the task that can be done in two minutes, and do only that. Then decide whether to go on.

uprooted.text: Being torn away from home — a move, emigration, the loss of familiar ground — is a real loss, and its painfulness is understandable. Badiou wrote a lot about people who found themselves far from their homeland, for example migrant workers in France. His political thesis goes like this: there is only one world, and everyone who lives in it belongs to it. For Badiou, truths don't belong to one nation or culture — they are universal and open to everyone. From this point of view, one could say that losing your ground does not take away your place in the world. You can carry with you what was an event for you — a love, a thought, a cause — and it remains yours in any language.
uprooted.practice: Write down one thing you brought with you on the inside — a habit, a song, a thought — that goes on living in you in the new place.

overload.text: Overload from the endless feed and informational noise is exhausting, and it is not your fault: that's how the environment is built. Badiou describes the "state of the situation" — an order that counts, names and classifies everything. From this point of view, one could say that the feed is the perfect machine for such counting: in it everything has already been named, rated and sorted into opinions. Badiou holds that behind the stream of "bodies and languages" it is easy to miss a truth — something genuinely new that can't be reduced to yet another opinion. Truth, in his view, is rare and requires concentration, not an endless stream. You can allow yourself to step out of the stream in order to notice the few things that really matter to you.
overload.practice: Close the feed for a couple of minutes and write down one thought or question that is truly yours, not something you've just heard.

unreality.text: The sense that everything somehow isn't real is a strange and sometimes frightening experience, and it deserves gentle treatment. In Logics of Worlds, Badiou distinguishes being from appearing: what is can appear in a particular world with different "intensity" — more strongly or more faintly. Existence in a world, for Badiou, is a matter of degree. From this point of view, one could say that the feeling of unreality resembles a moment when you, or the world around you, appear with very low intensity — muffled, as if from far away. But that doesn't mean you aren't there. Badiou stresses that the degree of appearing can change. Often it is brought back by simple, concrete things: a touch, a voice, a task.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a distinct texture — fabric, wood, cold water — and describe the sensation to yourself in three words.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious feeling, and it is worth simply living through it. Badiou is unexpectedly close to it here. His philosophy is built on the mathematics of sets, and he insists that infinity is not a privilege of God or an unreachable distance, but an ordinary property of being, of what is. From this point of view, one could say that awe is the moment when you suddenly notice this infinity right beside you — in the starry sky, in music, in another person's face. Badiou also considers art one of the four domains in which truth is born. Your awe is not just an emotion but a sign of meeting something greater than the usual order.
awe.practice: Stay with whatever filled you with awe for one more minute, doing nothing. Then write down one word that best describes the experience.

relief.text: Relief is a quiet and important feeling, and you can let it be there fully. In Theory of the Subject, Badiou describes anxiety as one of the affects that arise when the usual order cracks. From this point of view, one could say that relief is the moment when the tension lets go and you can breathe again. Fidelity, for Badiou, is long, everyday persistence, not a life of constant anxiety; there is room in it for a breather too. Relief shows how much strength was going into holding on. You can enjoy it without rushing to find the next task. A breather doesn't cancel what matters to you — it gives you the strength to keep going.
relief.practice: Take a deep breath in and a slow breath out, noticing where in your body things have eased. Tell yourself: "Now I can rest."

calm.text: Calm is a precious state, and you don't need to earn it. Badiou usually writes about intense moments — events, decisions, ruptures. But from the standpoint of his thought, one could say that calm also has its place in the life of a subject. Fidelity to an event, for Badiou, is not a series of flashes but a long, everyday continuation: quiet work, calm reliability, the day-to-day "holding on". Love for him is not only an encounter but also duration, a life shared over time. Calm can be exactly that kind of time: not emptiness, but the quiet steadiness of what you are faithful to. You can simply stay in it, adding nothing and not asking yourself whether you've done enough.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute, noticing what in your life is steady and reliable right now. Name it to yourself.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is the joyful feeling when something new suddenly becomes possible. Badiou names art as one of the four domains in which truths are born, alongside love, science and politics. For him, inspiration can be understood as an encounter with an event: something unforeseen opens a new way of seeing or doing. But Badiou also stresses the second part: an event lives only through fidelity to it, through the work that follows the flash. From this point of view, inspiration is not only a gift but also an invitation. You can enjoy it now and at the same time take a first step so that it doesn't remain just a moment. And it's all right if the flash fades later: for Badiou, fidelity rests not on the strength of a feeling but on carrying on.
inspiration.practice: Write the idea down while it's fresh, in one or two sentences. Note one small step that will carry it on tomorrow.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is one of those feelings that are embarrassing to admit even to yourself, but almost everyone knows it. Badiou distinguishes in a person the "human animal", concerned with survival, advantage and its place among others, from the "subject" that is born of fidelity to a truth. From Badiou's point of view, one could say that schadenfreude is the voice of precisely this animal: in a world where everything is compared, someone else's fall seems for a moment to lift us higher. There is nothing monstrous in this — only the logic of competition we are all built into. But Badiou reminds us that truths work differently: they don't divide people into winners and losers, and another's failure adds nothing to your life. Having noticed schadenfreude, you can ask: what race am I running right now — and do I need it?
schadenfreude.practice: Finish the sentence: "It felt good because in this comparison I…". Then think about what you yourself are lacking in this race.

contempt.text: Contempt can be cold and convenient: it puts us above others and protects us from what hurt us. It's an understandable defence. But Badiou is a philosopher of the universal: in Saint Paul: The Foundation of Universalism he stresses that truth is addressed to all without exception, and in Ethics he affirms that any person is capable of becoming a subject, that is, of going beyond their habitual, "animal" life. From this point of view, one could say that contempt passes a final verdict on what can be seen in a person so far, and forgets what they are capable of. At the same time, contempt often guards something precious in you — for example, your fidelity to honesty or to a cause. It helps to make out that value: then you can hold on to it without turning the other person into a nobody.
contempt.practice: Write: "What I despise in this person is…", and below it: "So what matters to me is…". The second line will tell you more about yourself than the first.

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong bodily reaction: you want to pull away, not see, not touch. It can be directed at people, at a situation, even at yourself, and in every case it isn't chosen. Badiou didn't write about disgust, but in Logics of Worlds he has the concept of "the inexistent": in every world there is something that is present yet barely admitted into visibility, as if it weren't there. From Badiou's point of view, one could say that disgust pushes something into the zone of the inexistent: this must not appear. When disgust is turned on a part of yourself, it's as if you deny that part the right to exist. But for Badiou it is precisely the inexistent that may turn out to be the place where something new begins. Perhaps what makes you feel disgust with yourself deserves not banishment but an attentive, calm look.
disgust.practice: Name in one word what disgusts you. Ask yourself: what do I want to push away from myself with this disgust?

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is usually born of real pain: you were treated unjustly, and something inside demands that the balance be restored. This feeling has a right to exist. In Theory of the Subject, Badiou names justice as one of the four affects of the subject, but justice for him is not returning the blow; it is creating something new in which the old injustice is no longer possible. From this point of view, one could say that revenge is built as repetition: it mirrors the wound and ties you to the one who inflicted it. Badiou is always interested in breaking with repetition. Acknowledging the wish for revenge is honest; listening to what it protects is useful. Usually beneath it lies the need to be recognized — for your pain to matter. That need can be respected without causing anyone harm.
revenge.practice: Write not about what should happen to the one who hurt you, but about what needs to be restored for you. What is the single most important word there?

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to us can be especially sharp, and afterwards shame often comes: how could I snap like that at someone I love? This is a very human story. In In Praise of Love, Badiou describes love as a "scene of the Two": an experience in which the world is seen not from one point of view but from two different ones. He stresses that love is neither a merger nor an idyll, but a long construction in which difference never disappears. Badiou was writing about love between partners, but from this point of view the same can be said about any closeness: anger is a sign that there are two of you and that your views have collided. It doesn't refute love. Fidelity, for Badiou, is not the absence of conflicts but the return to the shared construction after them. Anger gives no right to wound, but it doesn't make you a bad person either.
anger_at_loved.practice: Once things are calmer, finish the sentence: "At that moment I wanted you to see…". It could become the start of a conversation.

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and at the same time not being able to stand them is hard, and it seems that one feeling must be "real" and the other false. But this happens very often. Badiou, drawing on Lacan, describes the subject as split: it is never fully whole. And love, for him, is a "scene of the Two" in which the difference between two people doesn't dissolve but keeps working. From this point of view, one could say that mixed feelings are not a breakdown of love but a trace of that very difference: the other person never fully coincides with your expectations. Fidelity, for Badiou, doesn't require a single, pure feeling — it rests on the decision to keep going, not on the absence of doubts. You can let both feelings be and not hurry to choose between them.
ambivalence.practice: Write two lines: "What I love in you is…" and "What I can't stand in you is…". Just look at them side by side, deciding nothing.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, a departure or even the death of a seriously ill loved one often comes together with shame: how can I feel relief if I loved them? You can. In Ethics, Badiou criticizes a view that reduces a person to suffering and sacrifice, as if the worth of a life were measured by how much you have endured. Badiou also has the notion of the "human animal" — the part of us that simply wants to survive, to rest, to stop being under strain. Relief is its legitimate voice. From this point of view, one could say that relief and love live on different levels and don't cancel each other out. Your fidelity to what was real in that relationship continues regardless of what your body is breathing out right now.
guilty_relief.practice: Write down one thing that was real between you. Relief doesn't erase it — it stays with you.

indifference.text: Sometimes something "should" move you, yet inside all is quiet, and that feels awkward. In Ethics, Badiou criticized ready-made, "consensus" morality, which prescribes in advance what to feel and when — for example, a show of compassion at the sight of others' misfortunes. For him, truth begins not with an obligatory emotion but with an event: an unexpected encounter that really takes hold of you. Events are rare; most of the time we live in the ordinary order of things, which Badiou calls the "state of the situation". From this point of view, one could say that indifference is not a moral flaw but honest testimony: right now this hasn't taken hold of you. Faking a feeling is worse than admitting its absence. Sometimes indifference is tiredness, sometimes protection; either way it doesn't define who you are.
indifference.practice: Ask yourself, without judging: what touches me right now, even a little? Write it down, even if it seems small.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything — your job, your city, your usual role — usually means that your old life has become too tight. That is an important signal, not a whim. Badiou distinguishes a simple change of scenery from a real break — an event after which a new possibility appears. He called the habitual order of things the "state of the situation": everything in it is counted and put in its place, and sometimes there's no air to breathe. From this point of view, one could say that the dream of running away is a longing for an event, for something that will finally lead beyond what has been counted. Badiou gives no recipe for "leave or stay". But he offers a question: what do I want to be faithful to? The answer may turn out to matter more than an address — and hint at what change you really need.
escape.practice: Finish two sentences: "I want to run away from…" and "I want to run away to…". See which of them feels more alive.

forbidden_attraction.text: Being drawn to someone who is unavailable or "not the right one" can be confusing and frightening: as if you aren't in charge of your own feelings. In part, that's true. In In Praise of Love, Badiou stresses that everything begins with an encounter — a chance that can't be planned or forbidden in advance. He distinguishes the event of the encounter itself from what comes after: a decision, a declaration, a long construction for which a person is responsible. From this point of view, one could say that attraction in itself is neither an act nor a verdict, but a sign that something in you has responded. Badiou also distinguishes desire, which is directed at an image, from love, which is directed at the whole person. There's no need to rush to conclusions: you can simply explore what exactly in this encounter has touched you so much.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down which qualities, or what kind of life, you see in this person. Ask: what does this say about me?

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment is exhausting: it seems as if someone is weighing your every step. This feeling is very common. Badiou says that every situation has its "state" — a system of accounting that counts everyone, classifies them and places them in the right box. Under the gaze of others we keenly feel ourselves being counted. But for Badiou a subject can't be reduced to how it is counted: there is always something in a person that fits into no box. In Theory of the Subject he lists anxiety and courage among the affects of the subject, and understands courage not as the absence of fear but as the capacity to hold your ground when you are afraid. From this point of view, you don't have to wait for the fear to disappear; you can take a very small step together with it.
social_anxiety.practice: Choose one tiny action for today — saying hello, asking a question. Do it, allowing yourself to feel nervous.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is hard: you want to know how things will end, and it's impossible to know. Badiou argues that this is exactly how everything genuinely new works. An event, in his view, is "undecidable": at the moment it happens, it can't be proven that it matters or where it will lead. A person can only make a wager — here Badiou recalls Pascal's wager — and then, step by step, test its consequences. From this point of view, uncertainty doesn't mean you prepared badly or are living wrongly. It is the common condition of any beginning: in love, in work, in changing your life. Badiou calls the work that follows an event "fidelity", and this fidelity doesn't require knowing the outcome in advance. It requires only the next step.
uncertainty.practice: Without trying to guess the outcome, write down one small step that makes sense whichever way things go.

waiting.text: Waiting — for results, an answer, news — stretches time and doesn't let you focus on anything. It is a legitimately hard state. Badiou distinguishes what doesn't depend on us from what we do in response. A committee's decision, a phone call, a diagnosis — all of this comes from outside, and you can't influence it. But the life of a subject, for Badiou, is built not out of waiting for a verdict but out of fidelity to what is dear to you: people, a cause, a thought. Badiou wrote a lot about Beckett and saw in his characters, who keep walking and talking no matter what, not despair but the stubborn strength of desire. From this point of view, one could say that while the answer hasn't come, there is something that goes on regardless of it. Waiting does not cancel your life.
waiting.practice: Do one small thing right now that matters to you whatever the answer. Note that it is already done.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn't do can come back again and again. It is a sign that something mattered to you. In Logics of Worlds, Badiou describes moments of choice as "points" where the world demands a simple "yes" or "no", and he admits that people sometimes back away. But he also has a hopeful idea — "reactivation": a truth, once it has appeared, doesn't vanish without a trace; it can be returned to later, in other circumstances, in another form. From this point of view, one could say that a missed opportunity isn't closed forever: what was precious in it — courage, love, a cause — can come alive in your life in a different way. Regret then becomes not a verdict but a memory of what you still want to be faithful to.
regret.practice: Name what exactly was precious in what you missed. Where could that precious thing appear in your life now, even in another form?

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is one of the most recognizable pains: it is precisely their voice, their gaze, their presence that you miss. In In Praise of Love, Badiou describes love as a "scene of the Two": an experience in which the world is seen from two points of view at once. Whoever has once looked at the world that way no longer sees it as before. From this point of view, one could say that longing is the scene of the Two continuing in absence: you still see the world through that person's eyes too, and so their absence is felt everywhere. It hurts, but it is also evidence that the encounter was real. Badiou says that a truth born in love doesn't vanish without a trace. Longing is one form of fidelity, and you don't have to hurry it.
longing.practice: Write down one thing you see differently because of this person. That is what has stayed with you.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from hard news, war, injustice — shows that you care about what happens to people you will never meet. It is a precious feeling, though hard to carry. Badiou is a philosopher of the universal: for him truths are addressed to everyone, and humanity doesn't end at the borders of your own circle. But in Ethics he also warns about something else: when people turn into nothing but victims on a screen, and we into helpless spectators, compassion easily becomes passive and draining. From this point of view, one could say that pain for the world is easier to carry if it is tied not only to the stream of images but also to something you can do in your own world — help, support, be there. Even a small action changes the position of the spectator.
world_pain.practice: Limit your time with the news today, and choose one concrete small act of care for someone near you.

rejection.text: Rejection wounds painfully: it seems you've been refused not one thing but yourself as a whole. This feeling is understandable. In In Praise of Love, Badiou argues with the idea of "love without risk" promised by dating services — love insured against pain and failure. For him, meeting another person is always risky, and that is its value: love begins with a chance that can't be guaranteed. From this point of view, one could say that rejection is the price of the risk you took by opening up to another person. It is not proof of your insignificance but a trace of your courage. The encounter didn't become a "scene of the Two", but your capacity for encounter hasn't gone anywhere. Rejection closes one door, but it doesn't make you someone incapable of loving and being loved.
rejection.practice: Write down the risk you took. Admit to yourself: "I opened up — and that was brave."

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can live in the body constantly, even when everything seems fine. It is not a weakness but a deep need for a reliable bond. Badiou describes love as a long construction, but honestly admits that it comes with no guarantees; it is neither a contract nor an insurance policy. That is precisely why it requires fidelity — a daily carrying-on that no one can secure in advance. From this point of view, one could say that the fear of abandonment is the flip side of how much the lastingness of a bond means to you. But Badiou also offers another support: a subject is held up not only by someone holding on to them, but also by their own fidelity — to people, a cause, a thought. That fidelity belongs to you, and no one can take it from you.
abandonment.practice: Name three things you are faithful to regardless of other people. Say them to yourself, as a support.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love combines the strength of a feeling with its impossibility — it is agonizing. For Badiou, love in the full sense is a "scene of the Two", a construction that two people create together. From this point of view, one could say that in unrequited love the encounter happened on one side only, and the Two did not come together. This is neither a mistake nor a fault: such a construction simply can't be built alone, however strongly you love. But what you have lived through is not empty. Badiou says that love is an experience of the world from the point of view of difference, and you have already learned how strongly you can be taken hold of by another person. That capacity remains yours, even if this person did not respond.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love has taught you about yourself. Let it be one honest sentence.

humiliation.text: Humiliation wounds deeply: someone tried to make you smaller than you are. It is a serious experience, and you have a right to your pain. In Ethics, Badiou objects to seeing a person only as a victim, a creature who can be humiliated and reduced to their vulnerability. For him there is something in a human being that he calls "the Immortal" — the capacity to be greater than the circumstances one is put in. From this point of view, one could say that humiliation speaks about the situation and about those who humiliated you, but it passes no final verdict on you. It tries to put you in the box marked "nothing", but you don't fit in that box. Your dignity is not cancelled by having been treated badly.
humiliation.practice: Write down one thing you value in yourself that this event cannot cancel. Reread it slowly.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is very common, and it can easily colour a whole day. There is nothing shameful in it. Badiou, following Lacan, criticizes the "service of goods" — a life in which everything, bodies included, is assessed like merchandise against a market standard. Dissatisfaction with the body is often born right there: in comparison with a model designed so that you won't match it. In Logics of Worlds, Badiou speaks about the body differently: a body matters because it can carry a truth into the world — it lets you hug, work, create, be there for someone. From this point of view, one could say that the value of the body lies not in meeting a standard but in the fact that through it you take part in life. This doesn't require you to love it straight away — only to see it from another side.
body_shame.practice: Write down one thing your body helped you do today. Thank it for that — even if only in your thoughts.

illness.text: Illness, when your body lets you down, narrows the world and takes your strength — it is hard, and you have every right to be tired and upset. Badiou argued with philosophies that define a human being above all through vulnerability and mortality. He doesn't deny the fragility of the body, but says a person can't be reduced to it: there is in us a capacity to be faithful to love, to thought, to people — and that fidelity doesn't depend on how healthy the body is. From this point of view, one could say that illness changes the forms of your life but doesn't cancel what is dear to you. Badiou admired Beckett, whose characters, barely able to move, still carry on — talking, desiring, searching. Sometimes fidelity simply means carrying on as far as you can today.
illness.practice: Note one thing that remains dear to you today despite the illness. Give it at least a minute.

quote.text: …you must go on, I can't go on, I'll go on.
quote.author: Samuel Beckett

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a good, well-earned feeling, and there's no need to be embarrassed by it. In Theory of the Subject, Badiou names courage and justice among the affects of the subject: they are what a person experiences when holding fast in fidelity to their cause. And in later texts he speaks of "real happiness" — the joy that comes from taking part in something greater than survival. From this point of view, one could say that healthy pride is a sign that for a while you were a subject, not just someone who completed a task: you showed persistence, saw it through, stayed faithful to what you set out to do. Badiou values precisely this work that follows the flash of inspiration. Let yourself enjoy the pride — it confirms that such fidelity is within your reach.
pride.practice: Write down what exactly you had to overcome to do this. Read it to yourself with respect.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness — a quiet feeling in which sorrow is mixed with tenderness — doesn't need fixing. Badiou didn't write about melancholy specifically, and his philosophy rather calls to action. But from the standpoint of his thought, one could say that melancholy is a sensitivity to what has no place in the habitual order of things. Badiou calls this order the "state of the situation": everything in it is counted, but not everything fits in it. Gentle sadness seems to remember that life is larger than what has been counted — past encounters, possibilities never realized. And his idea of "reactivation" says that a past in which there was something genuine can come alive again. From this point of view, melancholy is not a dead end but a careful keeping of what may yet return.
melancholy.practice: Stay in this mood for a couple of minutes, with music or by a window. Ask yourself: what exactly is this tender sadness about?
